sections.summary: The neutral reading found that the recipients are described with three passive participles -- called, beloved in God the Father, and kept for Jesus Christ -- establishing their identity as people upon whom God has acted.
sections.relevance: The salutation describes the recipients' status entirely in terms of divine action: God called them, God loved them, God keeps them. The verb tereo ('to keep, guard, preserve') is passive -- the recipients are being kept by God for Jesus Christ. This supports permanence by grounding the community's security in God's initiative rather than in their own performance. However, the neutral reading noted that this same verb tereo will become structurally central to the letter, used both for God's keeping of the faithful (v. 1) and for the imprisonment of the angels who abandoned their station (v. 6) and the darkness reserved for wandering stars (v. 13). The verb's dual use establishes that being 'kept' can go two directions depending on whether one maintains or abandons one's assigned position.
key_phrases: called
beloved in God the Father
kept for Jesus Christ

sections.section_title: The Occasion -- An Intended Letter Displaced by Urgency
sections.summary: The neutral reading found that Jude changed his writing plans because infiltrators have crept into the community who pervert God's grace into sensuality and deny the only Master and Lord Jesus Christ, necessitating urgent contention for the faith once for all delivered to the saints.
sections.relevance: The passage implies that the faith delivered to the community can be successfully assaulted from within. The infiltrators are not external attackers but people who 'crept in unnoticed' and are operating within the community. Their specific error -- converting grace into a license for indulgence -- demonstrates that grace received can be distorted into something destructive. The call to 'contend for the faith' (epagonizomai, athletic competition language) presupposes that the faith must be actively defended and can be lost through passive negligence. The infiltrators' denial of the Master through their conduct (their verbal profession may remain intact while their behavior contradicts it) shows that standing before God can be functionally forfeited through the way one lives.
key_phrases: contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints
certain people have crept in unnoticed
who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality
deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ

sections.summary: The neutral reading found three precedents establishing that no status protects against judgment when faithfulness is abandoned: the exodus generation (God's delivered people, destroyed for unbelief after rescue), the angels (exalted beings imprisoned for abandoning their assigned station), and Sodom and Gomorrah (annihilated for crossing created boundaries into depravity).
sections.relevance: This passage directly addresses whether those who have received God's salvation can subsequently be destroyed. The exodus generation example is the most consequential: 'the same agent who saved also destroyed' -- these were God's covenant people who saw the plagues, crossed the sea, received manna, and heard the voice at Sinai, yet were destroyed for unbelief. The neutral reading stated explicitly: 'being among the saved people does not immunize a person against destruction' and 'salvation received does not equal salvation completed.' The three examples together demonstrate that neither covenant membership (exodus generation), nor exalted heavenly position (angels), nor civic existence (Sodom) protects against judgment when faithfulness is abandoned. The verb tereo creates a devastating wordplay: the angels who did not 'keep' their position are now 'kept' in chains, paralleling the recipients who are 'kept for Jesus Christ' (v. 1) -- being kept can go either direction depending on whether one maintains or abandons one's station.
key_phrases: Jesus, who saved a people out of the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe
the angels who did not keep their own position of authority
he has kept in eternal chains under gloomy darkness
Sodom and Gomorrah... serve as an example by undergoing a punishment of eternal fire

sections.section_title: Application to the Infiltrators -- Their Character Exposed
sections.summary: The neutral reading found that the infiltrators recapitulate every pattern from the historical precedents -- defiling flesh (Sodom), rejecting authority (angels), blaspheming the glorious ones -- and are further compared to Cain (defiance of God's warning), Balaam (corruption of spiritual authority for profit), and Korah (rejection of divinely established leadership), with extended metaphors describing them as hidden reefs at the community's love feasts, self-feeding shepherds, waterless clouds, fruitless trees twice dead and uprooted, and wandering stars for whom darkness has been reserved forever.
sections.relevance: The passage demonstrates that the infiltrators -- people present within the community, participating in its love feasts -- match every pattern of rebellion that brought judgment in the historical examples. The description 'twice dead, uprooted' about fruitless trees is particularly significant: it implies a finality beyond recovery. The neutral reading noted that every descriptor in verse 16 maps back to the earlier examples, demonstrating that the infiltrators are not merely flawed community members but people who have recapitulated the full pattern of covenant rebellion. The fact that these people are present 'at your love feasts' confirms they operate from within the believing community, and the darkness 'reserved' (teteretai, perfect passive of tereo) for them shows the same 'keeping' verb used for the community's security (v. 1) now applied to their judgment.
key_phrases: these are hidden reefs at your love feasts
shepherds feeding themselves
fruitless trees in late autumn, twice dead, uprooted
wandering stars, for whom the gloom of utter darkness has been reserved forever
woe to them! For they walked in the way of Cain

sections.summary: The neutral reading found that Jude cites 1 Enoch 1:9 to declare that the Lord comes with his holy ones to execute judgment on all the ungodly -- with fourfold repetition of 'ungodly' hammering the letter's signature term -- and applies it to the infiltrators as grumblers, malcontents, and loud-mouthed boasters who follow their own desires and show favoritism for gain.

sections.section_title: The Apostolic Warning -- This Was Predicted
sections.summary: The neutral reading found that Jude reminds the recipients of the apostles' prediction that scoffers following their own ungodly passions would arise in the last time, and identifies the infiltrators as those who cause divisions, are worldly (psychikoi), and are devoid of the Spirit.

sections.section_title: Instructions to the Faithful -- Keep Yourselves in the Love of God
sections.summary: The neutral reading found that the recipients are commanded to keep themselves in the love of God (using the letter's key verb tereo in the active imperative), building on their most holy faith, praying in the Spirit, and waiting for mercy that leads to eternal life, while exercising differentiated mercy toward those at various stages of being drawn away -- mercy on the doubting, snatching from the fire those in immediate danger, and showing mercy with fear toward the deeply contaminated.
sections.relevance: This passage directly addresses the believer's active responsibility for maintaining standing. The main verb 'keep yourselves' (heautous teresate) is the imperative of tereo -- the letter's structurally central verb. In verse 1, the recipients were described as 'kept for Jesus Christ' (passive -- God does the keeping); here they are told to 'keep yourselves' (active -- they must participate). The neutral reading stated: 'Both are true simultaneously. God keeps them (v. 1) and they must keep themselves (v. 21).' The community must remain within 'the love of God' -- they are to stay positioned within God's love, implying they can wander out of it. The three participial phrases (building, praying, waiting) describe the means of keeping. The waiting 'for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life' presents eternal life as a destination toward which mercy carries them, not a possession to be taken for granted. The three-tiered response to those at risk -- especially 'save others by snatching them out of the fire' -- presupposes that community members can be on the path to destruction and need active rescue.
key_phrases: keep yourselves in the love of God
waiting for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life
save others by snatching them out of the fire
have mercy on those who doubt
to others show mercy with fear, hating even the garment stained by the flesh

sections.section_title: The Doxology -- God's Power to Keep
sections.summary: The neutral reading found that the doxology ascribes to God the ability to keep the faithful from stumbling and to present them blameless before his glory with great joy, ascribing to the only God and Savior glory, majesty, dominion, and authority through all time.
sections.relevance: This passage is conventionally cited to support permanence: God is 'able to keep you from stumbling' (to dynamento phylaxai hymas aptaistous). After a letter filled with examples of catastrophic falling -- the exodus generation, the angels, Sodom, Cain, Balaam, Korah -- the assurance that God is able to prevent such falling is profoundly reassuring. The promise to 'present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy' envisions a successful eschatological outcome. However, the neutral reading noted that the key word is dynamento ('able') -- it describes God's power and capability, not an unconditional guarantee that operates regardless of the community's response. The letter has just spent 23 verses demonstrating that God's people can fall catastrophically (vv. 5-7) and that the community must actively 'keep yourselves in the love of God' (v. 21). The doxology completes the tereo frame -- God's keeping power is real and sufficient -- but the letter as a whole argues that the community's participation (building, praying, waiting, keeping) is also required.
key_phrases: to him who is able to keep you from stumbling
to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy
to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord
